scores.why: The note's age is in its outline: tips retreat by their own angle and 'every corner rounds', and a repeat 're-sharpens in one step', which is the clearest repeat in the frost essay. Weak spot for a pianist: in a chord 'neighbours merge into one hard spiked mass', so the notes of a chord cannot be counted. The 0.4 s rounding is slow next to the attack, though it only removes.

You count tiers directly, and a repeat shoves the column by an exact amount with 'zero overshoot, zero easing'. With 28 to 41 % of real notes repeating inside 0.5 s, columns will rocket off the top, and 70 to 79 distinct pitches squeeze a full part to about 15 px columns, so it suits picks. The 1 px hairs last 0.2 s and the 2 px bars that stay read as a stacked bar chart, not ice or rigidity.

The comb is really sharp, and the heavy tail ('every tenth 60..160 px') is why it looks real. Musically thin: x comes from a golden-ratio step on pitch class, so a melody zigzags and does not draw the 'one grain' the essay promises. The black slab wipes other clips on the shared canvas for two steps, so it is a bad neighbour in a layered scene.

The best decision is that the picture so far decides a note's length, so 'a loud note in a crowded place is a thick short stab'. A repeat as a parallel comb is countable. But pitch only sets a home x and a pitch-class direction, so you cannot follow a melody, and what you hear as a line does not look like a line. Near cracked glass by the author's own account, saved only by the three angles.

One line per note name is learnable, and the seam is whole in its step with no ease at all. But pitch class throws register away: a rising scale wraps round the stone, and an octave is only 'the same line with a different slide'. Permanent walking offsets also make the silhouette drift without meaning.

'An interval is literally visible as the angle between textures' is a real musician's idea, and a tritone as a right angle can be seen. A single dash is 1.5 px, and everything but 8 % is gone in two steps, so at real velocities (median about 60) it reads as fine glitter, not a sharp thing. Past three notes a chord becomes a general cross-hatch you cannot count.

The strongest repeat in the whole set: 'Counting is on, off, on', and a softer repeat leaves 'two lit slivers' so touch is visible. Repeats are about a third of real notes, so this matters. A band's tilt comes from pitch class by fifths, so neighbouring semitones cross, and a viewer would say velvet from the toothed edges alone. Dropping the body on a repeat bends P7, but the flash still lands at full.

A hard seam with no drawn line, 'only the place where two copies of the same fur disagree', is a surprise I believe. Musically it says little: pitch picks a patch, and the jolt reads the same for a melody note as for an inner voice. Two full-frame sprites baked from 40,000 hairs and a full pelt at rest are heavy for something meant to sit beside other widgets.

The reversed lighting is a real fact and a viewer would say fuzzy. A repeat 'bristling three times' is countable. Three stances over 0.14 s is a small staged sequence, 18 sprites of 512 px is a lot, and the dark fill covers other clips inside the form. A dark biomorphic shape ringed in hair should also be checked by eye for 'too suggestive'.

A long line with pitch as the place along it is a keyboard you already know, and the rise or fall of the melody combs the nap, which you could see. A repeat is 'a slap upright'. The teeth are the sharpest part and carry the word. It is one step from a spectrum meter, and the 0.6 s sweep of tips is visible motion after every note.

Fan width from the melody's bend is the one mapping here that shows phrase shape: 'a leap and a stepwise line look like different animals', and repeats are a row of closed brushes. It holds your interest because the row stays like a score. The row spacing comes from the clip's note count, so it wants picks. As texture it reads as tufts more than as rigid on elastic, because the body is never drawn.

filters: too_suggestive: a soft lobed dome with a wet colour swap and a dent with a dense lip; the author also lists this danger
scores.why: The two time scales are sensible, an instant dent over a slow register memory. But the dent is the same gesture for every note, and 'acid yellow-green' on a whole cushion is a big colour event for a small musical one. Two sprites per cushion plus clips and up to 750 ticks a frame is costly.

A repeat building 'a finger, one knuckle at a time' is a lovely record you can count afterwards. In the moment it is weak: lobes of 18 to 64 px at low brightness, and pitch class around a rim wraps the contour, so a melody does not read. Canvas masks with dilated cuts and a re-stamp on every backward seek are the most fragile drawing in this essay.

'The same constellation again' is how the ear hears a repeat, and an octave as parallel is something you notice unprompted. The redraw does count: at 12 repeats a second the old flecks have fallen to about 53 %, so the return is a visible flicker. Big shards in a power law carry a soft note, so velocity compression hurts little. Not one pixel moves, so it is perfect on snap, and a viewer would say sharp glitter.

filters: too_physical: flat umber, ochre and slate layers with sediment grain and a tilted unconformity is a geology diagram; the author also says it risks explaining how it works
scores.why: 'A silence happened here' is the best idea and it is rarely reached. At the median gap of 0.13 s a bed is about 12 px, so the stack hits the top in about 9 s and the tilt fires on height, not on a rest. Pitch is only one of six tones, so contour is lost and every note lands in the same place. The word rigid is not what a viewer says: they say barcode.

Sharpness earned by repetition: a repeat lands beside the last bite, 'so that the two arcs meet in a needle cusp', and you can read how often it sounded as long as the stone lasts. Notes subtract, which a musician feels. The problem is visibility: the default mass (40, 34, 44) at T 0.3 is about 12 of 255 on black, so the silhouette that holds the record barely shows; start from the oxblood stone. On a full part a stone lasts only a few seconds.

Keeps pitch as a position, so contour survives, and a rising run is 'a riffle, one thin leaf per note'. The flash and the crack are the same pixel, and moving along its own edge is a real answer to the ghost problem. It has the slash the user loved in casket. Registers the melody lives in shear into thin leaves with no code for it, and that is worth watching through a whole piece.

The fifths map makes a triad 'one small block' and a modulation move the digging, which a pianist would enjoy finding. But a scale jumps all over the map, so a melody is not followable. The drop is 6 to 22 px on near-black (wall 28, 24, 30), so after the flash very little is visible. Viewers will say tiles, not rigid.

filters: recipe: recursive rectangle splitting with a crack theme painted on; at the default `square` it is a Mondrian generator
scores.why: Recursive splitting of rectangles is a stock generative look, and at `square` 0.7 it is a Mondrian generator. A repeat as 'a narrowing ladder, each rung half the length of the last' is the musical part. Where a note lands depends on the largest cell, so the same pitch is never in the same place. Lit cells do give a note real area.

filters: too_physical: jigsaw grey plates with black furrows and an orange underlayer is bark; the author says it is the closest of the eight to a picture of its subject
scores.why: 'A note emits nothing. It uncovers a surface' is a good thought, and the orange shock is the most exciting colour in the essay. Nested terraces count repeats up to five. Pitch only picks a plate, and rough is not one of the user's four words.

A strip that 'rolls itself up the moment it is free' is a real elastic release, and a viewer would feel it. It is a staged little sequence, though: hold, roll, spiral grows, salmon exposed, over 0.25 s, so it reads as a small animation per note. In a fast run it is scaled down to short flicks, and the event is mostly lost. Cream and salmon strips look like skin, which should be checked by eye.

filters: fake_attack: a bud grows and a bridge thins before the note, which breaks P1 and is visible activity with no attack
too_suggestive: two round masses joined by a shaft, raised by the author too
scores.why: The most specific physics in the set, and 'the attack is the snap' makes you wait for each note, which is musical in a slow Chopin line. At the median gap of 0.13 s the thread lives about eight frames as a hair, so in most real music the idea is not there. The user has asked for no event without a note, and this one is built on foretelling.

The necking is the elastic thing, a ruled bar that 'cannot stay a bar', and it is what the eye gets. The 'loud means fewer' law is hard to perceive in real music: velocity 38 to 72 gives thickness 9 to 14 px, so 16 against 10 beads. A chord as coarse over fine and a repeat landing in the gaps both work, but velocity is carrying too much of the meaning.

'Regular in spacing and random in failure' is an observation only looking gives you, and the pelt exists only as tension, which earns the fuzzy and elastic pair. A repeat shuts the seam and tears it again, clearly countable. The snap times up to 0.14 s are a small scatter after the attack, and a dark red slab tearing with strands could read as a mouth, so check it.

One shape whose corners are the last three notes gives you short-term musical memory on screen, and a wide interval makes 'a long deep scoop'. A run flaps with 'one bright tip per note' that the eye follows, and a chord is a star cut back note by note, which feels like a resolution. Height is chosen for area, so only x carries pitch, and big flips at 12 a second need checking. Two to three fills is almost free.

filters: duplicate: a disc with a hard bright rim around a point is close to the dropped ripples even though it contracts, and the brief bans rings
scores.why: The contact-time law is true and nobody can hear or see it: nobody notices a soft and a loud note 'come home at the same moment'. A repeat is the same disc again. A clean disc against a cog of needles is the one good axis, and real notes do straddle its threshold at velocity 64. Viewers would say rings or gears, not elastic.

Straight to scribble in 150 ms, and 'a signature that never quite repeats', is the rubber band a viewer feels at once. Each note leaves a personal mark, which holds interest. Pitch sets only where it sits and a slant, so melody does not read, and a page of squiggles is close to scribble and calligraphy. Fast runs become 'a thicket of short slashes', still countable at the head.

A note taking away instead of adding is nice, and a run as 'a lane cut through the pelt' turns a passage into a place. But 2 to 4 px grains at 30 % look like static, not fur, and the hole only darkens at the canvas's own rate, so the attack is a ring of rim. The rim is irregular and stays in place, which keeps it off the ring ban, but the healing repaint is continuous and it needs a replay on seeks.

'A surface invisible until bent' is a beautiful idea, and the V cusps are very sharp at the moment of the strike. Every note makes the same mark at another place, gone by 0.3 s, so there is nothing to hold over a phrase. Velocity moves depth only, and depth compressed to the middle range gives little variety. 44 stacked lines moving over their own fade are a real moiré risk, and up to 2000 segments is on the heavy side.

Register as leverage is something a pianist feels at once: 'bass throws the entire picture and treble only flicks its end'. Rising bends up, falling bends down, a repeat 'worries the line back and forth', and a chord lands with one lit tick per note. It moves only on notes and wears only on notes. A combed line with barbs may read as a fishbone or a feather, which is why texture is only 6; it ranks this high for what it does with the music.

filters: too_suggestive: a V-shaped parting in an oxblood hair sheet with bright flanks is what essay 2 threw out as 'Parting'; slate or bone colour may rescue it
scores.why: 'White keys open the lower vane, black keys the upper' is the most pianistic rule in the set, and the crowding at the flanks gives real structure. A repeat re-opens a half-closed notch at full. The closing runs over 0.35 s as visible motion between notes, and the gap only goes black over 0.2 s.

Needle to coil with conserved length is a good drawing rule: low notes make loose scrolls and high notes tight ones, and two repeats 'curl to the other side'. A viewer would say spring. The note is a mark you read after it is over, and pitch carries x and size only. The tall low-note strip standing from the floor needs the check the author asks for.

The 1.5-node tooth is the most surprising decision in the essays: in a fast run 'the ghosts never clear and the rigid hatch turns into a fine fur', so speed itself becomes texture. One note, one tooth, whatever the velocity, so counting never saturates. A climb that ignores the melody's direction is odd for a musician, and the note's height is only in the chevrons. 1 px hairs at T 0.2 and crossing hatches need a moiré check.

filters: too_suggestive: dark red halves parting over a pale nap that spills across their edges; the author names the risk and only partly avoids it
scores.why: 'The contrast of those two edges is the widget', and hard against soft at the same moment is a real texture. But the loft is a second stage after the attack, and repeats counted by pieces of a broken slab are hard to read past two. Tack does the same thing with more reason.

'Soft is thread and loud is sheet' is a real velocity axis, and pitch as a tile with its own grain makes a chord a countable patchwork. A repeat mirrors the grain, which is a clean new-versus-same signal. The word it claims is hard to find: viewers see small hatched tiles in mint and violet, close to glitch blocks, and the palette is far from anything the user has liked.

filters: too_physical: a pale dome of spokes with tufts at the tips is a dandelion; the author names this as the real danger
scores.why: 'The picture is at its fullest before the music starts' is a beautiful idea, and a bald patch that widens counts a repeat. On a full part it thins to 140 of about 3,400 notes, and each wedge is three or four hairs, so the event is small. It also only ever gets emptier, which is hard to sustain through a long piece.

The refusal of the sine is the reason to exist: 'This one has no curve in it', and a piano player recognises a string whose length falls with pitch. A chord is strands flapping at different speeds, a repeat moves the pluck point by 0.07 so it is visibly new, and fast high notes are 'a spray of short high strands'. A roll spreads across the register as it should. The corner's run could read as a front, and the essay gives a fallback.

filters: duplicate: a thin branching lit path running from the struck thread out to the frame, whole on the attack, is close to the dropped chord lightning; only the slack threads set it apart
scores.why: The sag law is a real discovery, and 'the whole net knows at once' is a fine answer to fronts. You could learn a pitch as a shape, but only after many hearings, and 45 threads serve 70 or more pitches on a full part. Mostly it will look like thin lit wires, the 'dim wire diagram' the author fears.

A rising line turns 'like a clock hand', which is a pitch mapping you can follow from the first note, and one note crossing the whole screen with so few pixels is elegant. Chords get messy fast: a triad is six fans. The glitter while it swings adds new dashes after the attack, and everything radiates from one point, so check it does not read as a sunburst or as rings.

Pitch decides the thickness, so you 'read register off how a row is spaced', and a chord is a ratio of spacings, which is better for a musician than putting it on velocity. A hard cut on step 3 is honest and cannot be staged. The elastic claim then rests on a small oval ring, and the pale crescent makes each bead a drawing of a drop. Viewers will say dots.

The whole field turning on the note is the closest thing here to the collective feel of murmuration, and 'the spot itself stays black' gives every note a place you would not put a finger on. A repeat is a clench, and a run is 'a shudder of attention the eye follows across the screen'. Chords make sharp borders where needles disagree, so voices are countable as fists. It is close to a recipe on paper, but the turning toward saves it.

'You could read a note here with no change in brightness at all' is the right ambition, and a cut between combed and crossed is pure texture. Musically it is a patch at a place, the same gesture for everything, so it does less over a phrase than nap. Bone coverage of 22 % in a patch needs the budget rule, and five full-frame canvases are heavy.

Column by pitch class and row by octave is a real notation, and an octave as 'the same star twice' is readable. Stars on a grid are still close to decoration, and I doubt anyone learns twelve star fingerprints by eye during a piece. A repeat is flash, dim, flash, honest and rigid. The radials cutting out at 0.35 s happens during the fall and stays quiet.

The concave profile is the most convincing sharp in the set: 'under 2 px over the last 30 px', and a viewer feels it in a fingertip. It keeps handover's 'this note, then that one', which the user liked, and base width from the next gap means 'a semiquaver is a needle, a long note is a slab'. A shared aim point hides the chord's voicing, though you can still count thorns. Velocity moving the tip's x is the one mapping I would change.

The note is a change of texture: straight razors on the attack, wool by 0.4 s, and a repeat 'yanks the same ribbon straight again' in place, so every repeat can be counted. Pitch is real height, a chord is a stack of razors, and a run is 'a rain of straight sheaves' with only the newest one sharp. It answers fuzz against crisp-first with geometry. Reach runs only about 510 to 660 px across real velocities, so give it more gain, and test beating between lines.

The keyboard laid along a seam: bass left, treble right, a pair of needles per note, whole on the step, and a viewer would say it could hurt. A scale 'zips the seam shut', a repeat drives deeper, and Rachmaninoff's repeated chords would look like tighter blows. The ratchet stops at 200 px, about six repeats, then only the flash counts. They could read as teeth unless straight-sided and full height, and the withdrawal speeds up over 1.4 s, against P10, though it is dim by then.

'Brightness comes from density' with no stuff added, and the neighbours paying with wider gaps is a real elastic feel. A run fuses into a held slab, which is true of the muscle and interesting in a fast passage, though single notes then count only by flash. Real velocities give only 13 to 21 bars, so slabs stay narrow and alike. Only x carries pitch, and a comb over its own ghost must be tested for beating.

A repeated note is 'click, clack', and the picture is the record mod 2 of what was played, which is simple and very countable given how many repeats real pieces have. Heat length is a clear velocity axis. A roll flips bands one by one. It can go static under dense music, and straight chevron bands read as graphic rather than elastic.

filters: fake_attack: the needle visibly leans back before each note, 'a deliberate exception' by the author's words; load = 0 removes it
scores.why: 'The silence before a note is what charges it' is musical, and a first note after a breath landing big is rubato you can see. In a run the gap of 0.13 s gives only about a 15 degree throw with a 0.11 s lean before it, so needles never rest. The sector is a generic wedge, and rigid plus elastic is carried by the description more than the picture.

Band width from the perimeter means a leap reads as strain, and a repeat 'moves nothing' and flashes in place, the cleanest same-versus-new signal in the essay. Peg height comes from a golden-ratio index, not pitch, so half the shape is arbitrary. It will look like a jumping polygon outline, and elastic is less obvious than in film.

'A solid slab reaching hairlines without ever being a dim slab' is a good answer to the fade, and a repeat shutting the slats is very clear. Age can be read by how open it is. The turn is a long tail at τ 0.22 s, and every note does the same thing wherever it lands. Close to blinds at the wrong angle, and the bone sheet needs watching for P12 on loud notes.

filters: fake_attack: a flyer moves all the time between notes and falls faster into each one, which is anticipation the author admits
recipe: one step from a karaoke bouncing ball, as the author says
scores.why: The law is neat but real music cancels it: at the median gap a hop rises about 3 px, so most of a piece is a skitter on the floor. A chord lands as 'one plank', so the notes cannot be counted. A small rectangle in the air does not read as elastic. The author says this should go first in a cull, and I agree.

A sparkling contour across the whole screen, 'one sparkling contour line', would be beautiful, and the same note gives the same sparks. But pitch goes to a tilt on arbitrary ground, so up is not up, intervals have no meaning, and you can only recognise a note after long exposure. Up to 2,500 segments plus a 24,000-flake table is heavy for a widget meant to sit beside others.

filters: too_physical: 70 faceted, lit rock sprites filling the frame are a picture of rocks and close in feel to shatter
scores.why: 'Fuzz is the same hard grains from further off' is a fine thought, and a repeat leaves a countable row of tufts. Every note is the same zoom-out, and the contraction may read as suction. A six-note chord is about 420 draws for 0.3 s and a fast run about 280 plus tufts, the worst budget apart from stillness.

Only two angles on the screen is a strong rigid rule, and chevrons count repeats like rings. But the big event is decided by the pile: 'a soft note on a pile at its limit can bring down a great deal', so the largest thing on screen often answers the smallest thing you heard. Fourteen heaps have to share 70 or more pitches on a full part, and it risks looking like a mountain range.

'The clock is counted in notes', so the picture ticks on every attack and is still between them, which is the honest answer to the dissolve the user disliked on Ivory. A slow melody gets long lives and a fast run short ones with no code for it, and you can read how many notes ago a slab was. At six attacks a second a slab is gone in about 1.3 s, so it is best on picks. The crumbled stage says sand; the word sharp is present only on the newest slab.

filters: duplicate: a full stripe field that jumps on each note sits on Riley and on the dropped moiré, and the fading ghost of the old lines is a second line set for 0.09 s
scores.why: The topology is an exquisite idea, and 'a fork is one extra line' is exact. To a musician it is a shudder of the whole field up to 20 times a second, and a dislocation among 22 px lines is something you have to be shown. The 640x360 upscale undercuts the knife crest it claims, and a phase field with a 3.7 MB table is a lot of machinery.

filters: duplicate: a bright branching zigzag whole on the attack is close to the dropped chord lightning, which the author flags
scores.why: 'The two hands push towards each other' is a real musical idea, and a repeat that 'rewires' is new and countable. Depth by velocity is visible. But each chain is a fresh random walk, so a pitch has only a start cell and the eye gets a bolt. Rigid is mostly a claim, because nothing moves and viewers see struts.

filters: duplicate: mathematical dot figures per pitch are the ghost of the dropped whitney, as the author says
scores.why: A chord is 'one figure, not several', which is lovely for harmony and fatal for counting its notes. A repeat pulling the grains tight is the one good moment. Above 8 notes a second it is cards being dealt, loosening takes half a second, and 4,000 to 5,600 rects a frame is over budget. A Chladni figure is also a stock science-museum image.

A comb like a music box or a harp: tines long in the bass and short at the top, so a rising run 'goes up the comb' and a rolled chord ripples as it should, which only pluck matches. A repeat whips to the other side, leaving countable clouds. The needle back in line and a soft cloud 'where the needle no longer is' give sharp and fuzzy in one look. A slow sink of 6 px a second is quiet, but the 0.25 s ring and cloud shot soften the snap; 24 tines want picks.

clusters.why: Almost one idea: 15 degrees per pitch class, parallel marks, a band by height. 3:mica wins because a repeat is the same constellation, which matches the ear, and the redraw still counts (old flecks are near 53 % at 12 a second), while its power-law shards give a sharper stroke than 1.5 px dashes.

Same name, different idea. 6:glint's clock hand is the most followable single line, but a triad is six fans and all of it radiates from one point. 1:glint keeps chords legible as an angle between textures, up to about three notes, and has no swing after the attack.

Both light a fixed set of flakes for a note, and the same note gives the same sparks. 3:mica keeps pitch meaningful, as height and as an angle, so octaves are visibly parallel. 8:mica's contour ribbon is the prettier picture, but pitch is a tilt on arbitrary ground and it costs far more to draw.

Both put a whole hairline on the step with no easing. 3:cleave keeps pitch as a position, so contour and register survive, and it explains why its motion leaves no smear. 1:cleave's pitch-class lines are learnable but fold every octave together.

The deciding question is what sets the spacing. In 6 it is mainly pitch, so register reads as spacing; in 4 it is velocity, whose real range gives only 16 against 10 beads. 4 has the better elastic moment (the visible neck) and should lend it, but 6 is more musical and has no staged step.

Both are lines that end on other lines. 1:stopdead has tapered needles, two kinds of end and a home by pitch, and its three angles look like a crystal; 3:tjoints is recursive rectangle splitting with a nice repeat ladder, and its notes have no fixed place.

Both split a dark red slab with fibres in the gap. Tack's repeat shuts the seam and tears again, which is simpler to count than suture's added seams and pieces, and its pelt only exists under tension. Suture also carries the stronger suggestive risk.

All make texture the envelope, sharp first and softer later. Crimp is the simplest and has the best repeat, razor again in place, with pitch as true height. Sublimate is next but its chord merges; cut is the most honest about time; stillness and handlens are over budget and lose the notes.

All change a patch inside a fixed pelt. Nap's second touch erases the first, so its picture holds a record and a repeat is an off switch. Twitch has the best motion but says less about the note, bristle is the cheapest pure cut, flinch's pelt looks like static, and unzip has the pianist's white and black key rule but a suggestive shape.

All are struck lines. Catkin leaves a counted memory beside the line and lays pitch out as a comb, so runs and rolled chords read best. Pluck is the most specific and the purest line and would be my second; snapback leaves the most personal mark but no pitch sense.

All count notes by stacking or ratcheting. Awn's one tooth per note never saturates and turns speed into fuzz; needleice is the plainest count but a bar chart; causeway goes dark; repose's slides do not match what you hear.

One shape held by the last few notes. Film has the needle corners and scoops that give it texture and show intervals in the edge. Sinew has the better repeat (nothing moves, a flash in place) and film should consider borrowing it.
Notes that take away. Knap's bites make teeth from repeats and sharpen the form; clock is too literally a dandelion and only empties; flinch's holes sit in static.
Hard hairs that rotate on a root. Urchin's field turning toward an empty spot has a collective feel and a threat that hackles' line of teeth lacks, although hackles has the clearer keyboard.

All read the future from CHORDS and move before a note, and all fail in the same way in real music, where the median gap is 0.09 to 0.19 s. With `load` at 0 latch still sets the throw from the silence, so only latch survives the no-fake-attacks rule.
A stress path lit through a fixed structure. Tensile has the sag law and a net that gives; load's two hands are a nice idea, but its random zigzags look like the dropped lightning.

A fixed map of cells, one per pitch. The fifths layout gives chords and keys a shape, which is worth more to a musician than a star fingerprint or a grain angle, though the cells must be brighter than the author's near-black.

overall: I measured the songs: the median gap is 0.09 to 0.19 s with peaks of 16 to 17 attacks a second, 28 to 41 % of notes repeat inside 0.5 s, and median (v/127)^1.5 is only 0.28 to 0.46. Against that, the set gets a lot right: nearly everything appears whole on the attack, nothing grows between notes, and most essays found real behaviour instead of a picture. Repeats are treated seriously, and the best ideas (crimp, nap, quill, buckle, knap) give a repeat its own meaning. What it keeps getting wrong: laws that are true but cannot be perceived (pancake's contact time, 4:beading's loud-means-fewer, forks' topology, areole's fingerprints); ideas tuned for the slow case that vanish at real density (neck, hop, beds' silence, latch); velocity ranges designed for 0 to 127 when real notes live in the middle, so soft-versus-loud contrasts need more gain; very dark bodies whose record cannot be seen (knap, causeway); and pitch given to a hash or a fold so that a melody does not read as a melody. Many fuzz ideas also spend their whole cost on a full-frame sprite and would be heavy beside other widgets. I ranked the top 12 by musicality first, with texture as the tiebreak, so an idea can sit below others that total higher on the other criteria. Near misses for my top 12 are setae (the only one that shows phrase shape), awn, striation, knap and cut. The 'thrown out' and 'left out' lists at the ends of essays 2 and 4 are not ideas and are not scored; the authors were right to leave them out.
